newsitem.title: USA: Iraq nearing limit of U.N. oil sales plan.
newsitem.headline: Iraq nearing limit of U.N. oil sales plan.

text.p: Ten days after the Iraqi oil-for-food plan went into effect, Baghdad has signed nearly enough oil contracts to fulfil the amount of sales allowed by the United Nations for the next six months.

As a result, industry and U.N. sources said on Friday that the United Nations was holding up approval of some contracts submitted by Iraq, concerned that Baghdad's deals may exceed the $2 billion worth of oil it may sell over six months in order to buy humanitarian goods.
The oil-for-food agreement between Iraq and the United Nations went into effect on Dec. 10 to ease the impact of stringent trade sanctions imposed in August 1990 when Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait.

To date, 16 contracts have been approved by oil experts or overseers hired by the United Nations. But Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) has signed contracts with at least four other companies and is in negotiations with another three, according to oil industry sources.

Calculations by Reuters show the total contracts approved so far amount to 534,000 bpd. If the current reltively high oil prices are sustained, Iraq's signed and pending contracts would be well above the $2 billion limit.

Germany's ambassador, Tono Eitel, chairman of the U.N. Security Council's sanctions committee on Iraq, acknowledged that the overseers were considering scaling back the amount contracted by 10 percent.

Another diplomat said that the overseers were aware that if the amount sold "slips just over the $2 billion then in international law it is illegal," a reference to the 1995 Security Council resolution that set the amount.
Since the plan went into effect, SOMO has signed contacts with about 20 oil companies from the United States, Europe, Turkey, Russia and Japan.

Contracts are based on formulas that set the price at a discount to various world benchmark oil prices on the day the oil is due to be shipped, including West Texas Intermediate crude in the United States.
